title: The Fed Hikes, Yields Hit 5%, but Tech Refuses to Break
deck: The Federal Reserve raised interest rates this week, but technology stocks remained resilient. Treasury yields approached 5%, oil stayed near $100, and investors became increasingly selective about which companies could withstand higher borrowing costs.

quickTake: The Federal Reserve raised its target federal-funds rate by 25 basis points to 3.75%-4.00%, its first increase since 2023.
The Nasdaq gained 0.7%, while the Dow declined 1.7% and the Russell 2000 fell 1.5%. Technology showed relative strength despite higher borrowing costs.
The 10-year Treasury yield briefly crossed 5% before finishing the week near 4.94%.
August retail sales increased 1.2%, suggesting that consumer spending remained resilient despite inflation and elevated energy costs.
WTI crude finished near $100 per barrel, keeping energy prices and their potential effects on inflation in focus.
Next week, investors will monitor Treasury yields, preliminary PMI data, jobless claims, housing activity, and Costco earnings.

sections.heading: 1. The Week in One Sentence
body: The Federal Reserve raised interest rates, Treasury yields approached 5%, and oil remained near $100 per barrel, yet technology stocks managed to finish the week higher.
The biggest development was the divergence between major equity indexes. The Nasdaq gained 0.7%, while the Dow fell 1.7% and the Russell 2000 declined 1.5%.
This divergence suggests that investors are becoming increasingly selective about which companies can maintain earnings growth and generate cash flow in a higher-interest-rate environment.
sections.callout: My takeaway: the market is increasingly focused on which businesses can sustain growth and profitability while borrowing costs remain elevated.

sections.heading: 2. The Federal Reserve Raises Interest Rates
body: The Federal Reserve raised its target federal-funds rate by 25 basis points to a range of 3.75%-4.00%. This marked the central bank's first rate increase since 2023.
The decision reflects continued concerns about inflation despite relatively resilient economic activity.
The Fed's latest economic projections anticipate 2.3% real GDP growth in 2026, a 4.1% unemployment rate, and 3.7% PCE inflation.
These projections suggest policymakers expect economic growth to continue while inflation remains above the Fed's 2% target.

Higher interest rates are intended to reduce inflation by making borrowing more expensive and slowing demand. However, tighter monetary policy can also create challenges for businesses that depend on financing and for investors holding stocks with expensive valuations.
The next Federal Reserve decisions will depend heavily on inflation, employment, and economic growth.
sections.callout: The key question is whether the Fed can bring inflation down without causing a significant slowdown in economic activity.

sections.heading: 3. Consumer Spending Remains Resilient
body: August retail sales increased 1.2%, while the retail-sales control group rose 1.4%. These figures suggest American consumers continued spending despite elevated energy prices and inflation.
The labor market also showed resilience. Initial unemployment claims declined to 196,000 for the week ending September 12.
A combination of strong consumer spending and relatively low unemployment claims gives the Federal Reserve additional room to maintain restrictive monetary policy.
However, continued consumer strength could also make inflation more difficult to bring back toward the Fed's target.
The important question is whether households can sustain their spending as higher borrowing costs gradually affect personal finances.

sections.heading: 4. Treasury Yields Approach 5%
body: The 10-year Treasury yield briefly crossed 5% during the week before finishing near 4.94%. The 2-year Treasury yield ended around 4.67%.
Higher Treasury yields influence borrowing costs throughout the economy, including mortgages, corporate debt, and consumer loans.
They also affect equity valuations. When investors can earn relatively high yields on government bonds, stocks must offer sufficiently attractive potential returns to justify their additional risk.

Growth companies are particularly sensitive because much of their valuation can depend on earnings expected several years into the future. Higher discount rates reduce the present value of those future earnings.
Housing is another sector exposed to rising yields. Higher mortgage rates can weaken affordability, reduce housing demand, and create additional pressure on homebuilders.
The 10-year Treasury yield will remain one of the most important indicators to monitor over the coming weeks.
sections.callout: The 5% Treasury threshold is an important level to watch because sustained higher yields could create additional pressure on equity valuations and borrowing costs.

sections.heading: 5. Technology Stocks Show Relative Strength
body: Despite the Federal Reserve's rate increase, the Nasdaq gained 0.7% this week, outperforming the Dow and Russell 2000.
Technology stocks showed greater resilience than several other areas of the market.
Artificial intelligence remains an important long-term investment theme, particularly for semiconductor manufacturers, cloud infrastructure providers, and software companies.
However, investors are increasingly focused on whether companies can convert AI-related spending into sustainable revenue growth, operating profits, and free cash flow.
Businesses with strong balance sheets and established earnings may be better positioned to manage elevated borrowing costs than companies that depend heavily on external financing.

The next stage of the AI investment cycle will require investors to distinguish between companies demonstrating measurable financial results and those relying primarily on expectations of future growth.
sections.callout: AI remains an important market theme, but actual earnings growth and free cash flow will be essential when evaluating whether current valuations are sustainable.

sections.heading: 6. Oil Prices Remain Near $100
body: WTI crude oil finished the week around $100.30 per barrel, gaining approximately 0.2%. Brent crude ended near $103.87, declining approximately 0.7%.
Despite relatively small weekly changes, oil experienced significant volatility.
Supply concerns surrounding Saudi Arabia's East-West pipeline pushed prices higher during the week before reports of a potential partial restart helped ease some concerns.
Elevated oil prices remain important because energy costs affect transportation, manufacturing, and consumer spending.
If oil prices remain high for an extended period, businesses may face increased operating expenses while households experience additional pressure on their budgets.
Persistent energy inflation could also complicate the Federal Reserve's efforts to bring overall inflation back toward its target.
Oil prices will remain an important variable for both monetary policy and corporate earnings.

sections.heading: 7. Gold Rebounds
body: Gold finished the week near $4,390.11 per ounce, gaining approximately 1%. The precious metal rebounded after three consecutive weekly declines.
Gold faces competing influences in the current environment.
Higher interest rates increase the opportunity cost of holding an asset that does not generate interest income.
However, geopolitical uncertainty and concerns about persistent inflation can support demand for gold as a defensive asset.
The direction of Treasury yields, the U.S. dollar, and geopolitical developments will remain important factors influencing gold prices.

sections.heading: 8. Earnings and Corporate Outlook
body: This week's market performance highlighted the importance of corporate earnings in a higher-rate environment.
Investors are increasingly focused on whether companies can maintain revenue growth, protect operating margins, and generate free cash flow despite elevated financing and input costs.
Technology companies continue attracting interest because of artificial intelligence investment, while consumer-facing businesses must demonstrate that demand remains resilient.
Looking ahead, Costco's upcoming earnings report on September 24 will provide another opportunity to evaluate consumer spending trends.
Investors should pay attention to comparable sales, membership growth, operating margins, and management commentary about consumer behavior.
Strong earnings results could support confidence in consumer resilience, while weaker guidance could raise questions about how long current spending trends can continue.

sections.heading: 9. What I'm Watching Next Week
body: 10-Year Treasury Yield: The 5% level remains an important market threshold. A sustained move above 5% could create additional valuation pressure, particularly for growth stocks and rate-sensitive sectors. A decline in yields could provide some relief for equities and borrowing costs.

September 23 - Preliminary PMI Data: Manufacturing and services PMI reports will provide insight into business activity. Investors will be looking for signs that higher interest rates and energy costs are beginning to slow economic growth.

September 24 - Initial Jobless Claims: Weekly unemployment claims will provide another indication of labor-market conditions. A sustained increase in claims could suggest that businesses are beginning to reduce hiring or employment.

September 24 - New Home Sales: Housing data will help investors evaluate the effects of elevated mortgage rates on demand. Weakening home sales could indicate that higher borrowing costs are increasingly affecting consumers.

September 24 - Costco Earnings: Costco's fiscal fourth-quarter earnings will offer additional information about consumer spending. Membership growth, comparable sales, operating margins, and management guidance will be particularly important.

sections.heading: Bottom Line
body: This week demonstrated that higher interest rates do not necessarily affect every part of the stock market equally.
The Federal Reserve raised rates, Treasury yields approached 5%, and oil remained near $100 per barrel. Yet the Nasdaq still finished higher.
Investors appear increasingly focused on businesses capable of maintaining earnings growth and generating cash flow in a challenging interest-rate environment.
Technology and artificial intelligence remain important market themes, but valuations will need to be supported by actual financial performance.
The three numbers I am watching most closely are the 10-year Treasury yield near 5%, oil prices around $100 per barrel, and the federal-funds target range of 3.75%-4.00%.
The central question for the coming weeks is whether economic growth and corporate earnings can remain resilient as monetary policy becomes more restrictive.
sections.callout: My final takeaway: higher rates are making earnings quality, balance-sheet strength, and cash flow increasingly important when evaluating individual companies.
